analysis.one_liner: Lets the FTC win refunds and disgorgement from fraudulent companies and lets the DOJ sue for antitrust damages on consumers' behalf.
analysis.headline: The bill was sent to the Senate Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After the Supreme Court's 2021 AMG Capital decision, the FTC could no longer win money back for consumers in federal court — it could only get court orders telling companies to stop. This bill would have restored that power, letting the FTC ask a court to order scammers to pay restitution, refund money, cancel contracts, and give up ill-gotten profits. It would also have let the Justice Department sue for antitrust damages on behalf of all U.S. consumers, so people hurt by price-fixing could recover money without filing their own lawsuits.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who lose money to fraud and deceptive marketing gain the most: the FTC could again seek court-ordered refunds, restitution, canceled contracts, and disgorgement of the profits companies made from a violation [S2][S3]. People harmed by antitrust violations also gain, because the bill lets the Justice Department bring a single civil action on behalf of all U.S. residents and recover their damages plus attorney's fees [S3]. The FTC itself gains a practical enforcement tool and a new option to refer competition cases to the Justice Department to collect actual damages [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers cheated by scams and price-fixing

how_it_helps.text: Lets the FTC ask a court to order companies that engaged in unfair or deceptive practices to pay restitution for consumer losses, rescind or reform contracts, and refund property [S2][S3].
Lets the FTC recover disgorgement — forcing companies to give up the profits they made from a violation — which the Supreme Court took away from the agency in its 2021 AMG Capital decision [S2][S3].

Lets the Justice Department bring a civil antitrust suit on behalf of all U.S. residents (a 'parens patriae' action), recovering consumers' damages and attorney's fees without each victim needing to sue individually [S3].
Stops violators from running out the clock by hiding abroad: any time a defendant spends outside the United States does not count toward the bill's 3-year deadline for seeking relief [S3].
Lets the FTC refer a won competition case to the Attorney General to collect actual damages under the Clayton Act, adding a monetary penalty to what is otherwise an injunction-only tool [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that engage in deceptive practices and their owners would pay: they could be ordered to return money to consumers, cancel contracts, and disgorge their net profits from the violation [S3]. Companies facing antitrust claims would face a new risk of government-filed damages suits on behalf of all affected consumers [S3]. Taxpayers bear no direct cost under the bill.
analysis.who_pays_short: Companies that deceive or overcharge consumers

drawbacks.text: The FTC must prove that a reasonable individual both knew the practice was unfair or deceptive and materially relied on it, and courts may not presume reliance just because a consumer was exposed to the practice — a proof burden that could defeat restitution in mass-deception cases where individual reliance is hard to show [S3].
The bill sets a 3-year deadline for seeking restitution and disgorgement, cutting off remedies for older misconduct [S3].
Disgorgement is capped at net profits directly related to the violation and is offset by any other money the court orders paid, limiting how much of the takings the FTC can claw back [S3].

Business defendants and their allies have long argued that broad disgorgement powers risk penalizing companies for conduct that is not clearly unlawful; this bill's reliance and burden-of-proof requirements are the kind of guardrails such critics demand, but they also narrow how much money consumers can actually recover [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On balance this would have been a net gain for consumers: it restores a money-recovery tool the Supreme Court removed in 2021, which is the only practical remedy in many fraud cases, and adds a government route to antitrust damages. The costs fall on companies that actually violate the law, not on ordinary people. The main caveat is that the bill's own guardrails — the reliance requirement, the 3-year limit, and the net-profit cap on disgorgement — mean it restores less power than the FTC had before 2021, so the help it offers is real but narrower than it first appears.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee the same day, and the committee never held a hearing or vote on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Mike Lee introduced the bill on March 30, 2023, with three Republican colleagues — Cruz, Hawley, and Blackburn — joining as original cosponsors [S3][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day; that was the only action the bill ever received [S5].
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill never reached the Senate floor before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that profit from deceptive practices are better off, because the FTC still cannot easily win court-ordered refunds or disgorgement from them, and consumers still have no government route to antitrust damages. The FTC and the Justice Department remain without the tools this bill would have given them.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Republicans, and the Democratic-led Commerce Committee never acted on the bill; no votes were ever recorded, so actual partisan support and opposition were never measured.

industries.industry: Direct-response marketers, telemarketers, and other repeat FTC deception defendants
industries.note: These are the companies the FTC's monetary remedies target; the bill would have exposed them to court-ordered restitution, refunds, contract cancellations, and giving up their profits from a violation [S3]. Consumers defrauded by them would recover money they otherwise keep losing.

industries.industry: Large firms exposed to antitrust claims (dominant platforms, price-fixing defendants)
industries.note: The bill would let the Justice Department sue for antitrust damages on behalf of all U.S. residents, creating a collective route for consumers to recover overcharges and raising litigation risk for dominant firms [S3].
